0203082 · 8 files
Body sync was verified working end to end - Room v60, write-through, merge pull, Realtime - and the eight server tables held ZERO rows while the phone held 42. Because write-through only pushes NEW writes. Every row created before it existed had no path to the server at all. Sync looked perfectly healthy the whole time: realtime connected, pull running each foreground, tests green. Wipe the device in that state and body, memory, lists, budgets, staples and goals are destroyed - with a success message. Same shape that left ledger_transactions and maintenance_schedules empty for a week with the data sitting on the phone. Seen twice today and still not generalised until the server came back zero. BodyBackfill sweeps every table for rows the server has never seen, per-table resumable cursor in the ObdSampleUploadCursor pattern, idempotent on the existing ON CONFLICT (origin_guid) upserts. It runs INLINE before the pull rather than fire-and-forget, because a pull that races an unsent local row will weigh last-write-wins against a server that has never heard of it. A row already soft-deleted locally and never synced is skipped, not pushed - softDelete matches on origin_guid and would no-op, and upserting first would resurrect it. A wipe only destroys what would otherwise survive. Also fixed, same class: NotesController.untick hard-deleted workout sets through the DAO, so a synced set's delete never reached the server and the row returned on the next pull. Routed through BodyWriteThrough. The template is four parts now, not three: write-through, BACKFILL, pull, realtime. The six remaining aspects inherit all four. Suite 2900, 0 failures. 9fc7141 · 16 files
Every appointment Kevin created by voice was invisible to the server. LiveToolbox.addAppointment inserted locally with a fake client-minted serverId - a real UUID that had never touched the server - and never called the backend at all. Only a Settings button moved them, so anything created between taps existed on exactly one device. addEvent now writes locally first (never blocking on the network) then pushes, and a new row carries a NULL serverId until a real round trip, so the pull's guid-first matching can adopt it later instead of pairing against a fake. Event.serverId is nullable; v58 to v59 rebuilds the table, since SQLite has no ALTER COLUMN. sync_outbox is generic on purpose - fleet and places have the same problem. A failed push enqueues rather than vanishing; the local write still lands so the UI stays honest. Drain happens BEFORE pull on foreground, because a local change must reach the server before the pull can weigh last-write-wins against it - reversed, your own edit loses to the copy it was meant to replace. Two things found by tracing rather than assumed, both worth keeping: EventsBackend.upsert is NOT idempotent - with a null serverId it unconditionally INSERTs, so every retry would have minted a duplicate server row. uploadMigratedEvent checks origin_guid first and genuinely is idempotent, so the drain uses that instead. 4xx and 5xx are indistinguishable here: SupabaseEventsBackend's translating helper collapses every RestException into one type and the HTTP status does not survive. "Never retry forever" is therefore a bounded attempt count, not error classification - a substitution, stated as one. NOT built, and both surfaced rather than decided: EngineNotesRetirementCopy still mints fake serverIds, but it is a one-time batch copier, not a live path. And NotesController.updateAppointment/removeAppointment stay local-only even on a configured install - that is a locked ruling from one-today ticket 02, and reversing it is Kevin's call, not a builder's. 2daeae4 · 6 files
Kevin: "can we have the app just sync to the backend live instead or something automatic." Nothing in this app has ever pulled server changes. The only path was a Settings button that uploads, wipes every kind='reminder' row, refills, and WITHHOLDS rows it cannot attribute - so they vanish from the phone instead of merely being unconfirmed. That is why 120 real coursework rows have sat on the server unseen: COSC 3334 Homework 1-6, both midterms, COSC 3318 FINAL EXAM, and COSC 4305 Report 1/7 through 7/7, the first of which is due Sep 4. EventsSync.pull merges instead. Server row with no local match is INSERTED. Both sides present resolves by last-write-wins on updatedAtMs - which was already set on every local write and had never once been compared. A server tombstone soft-deletes locally. And a local row the server lacks is LEFT ALONE: absence from the server is not evidence of deletion, and treating it as such is exactly how the coursework became invisible. This project already did that once without naming it: the gate lives in SQL and every client inherits it. Repeat the pattern, do not treat it as a special case. A routine sync may not perform an unbounded deletion
no ticket

Ticket 20 Q2. The retraction pass removed 213 rows in one run and reported it as one line inside a success message. Nothing stated the count before acting, nothing bounded it, and the damage surfaced only because the next run failed loudly on an unrelated index. Now it computes the candidate set first and always names it - including when the answer is none, which it never used to say. Under the bound it proceeds as before. At or over it, it retracts nothing, says how many looked orphaned and why, and states that running again confirms. The second run is the consent. The bound is relative, not a count: over a small absolute floor AND over a quarter of what is on the server. 213 of 354 is sixty percent and would have stopped; a handful out of a handful never trips it, because stopping for those trains 'yes' into a reflex. Consent remembers the exact set it withheld, so a later run with a materially different set refuses again instead of spending the earlier warning as blanket permission. No dialog, deliberately - the migration screen has none by design, and a modal that appears only on the dangerous path is one people learn to dismiss. A withheld retraction is Result.success with isClean false: the upload and refill did their work, an action was declined, and the wording never borrows the 'Did not finish' failure phrasing. 2,855 tests, 0 failures. That is the precise "row pointing at nothing" shape ticket 09 is named after, arrived at by design rather than by the uninstall the ticket investigated. Now the delete is conditional on there being somewhere durable to have put it. Deleting after a successful upload is right, because the bucket holds the copy and the local file is staging. Scoped bucket_id policies instead, reusing the existing is_household_member helper. And deliberately no update or delete policy: RLS default-deny then makes it impossible for anyone to silently replace or remove a photo a row still points at. PhotoFieldResolver gained a third state, ON_SERVER, because with the staging file legitimately gone after upload every healthy receipt would otherwise render as MISSING - a false claim of unrecoverability. Room v45 to v46 carries the fact needed to tell those two apart. No UI renders receipt photos yet, so that wording is exercised by tests rather than on a screen. Said plainly rather than implied. Make the suite green on purpose instead of by luck
hardening 13
9ae71c9 · 86 files
Six test classes leaked "Illegal connection pointer" out of Room's invalidation tracker onto an arch_disk_io thread, uncaught, and kotlinx-coroutines-test blamed whichever runTest started next. Which test died depended on execution order, so any change moved the casualty and every fix looked like it worked. Option 2 (synchronous disk IO) was disqualified on evidence: Room's assertNotMainThread checks Looper directly, not ArchTaskExecutor, and two tests already need allowMainThreadQueries because Robolectric's test thread IS the main-looper thread. It would have broken the 79-file surface that relies on hopping off that thread. The fix is a pool-quiescence barrier using only java.util.concurrent and ArchTaskExecutor's public Executor: submit one barrier task per pool thread, and the instant all are parked together, everything queued before them is provably done. No Room internals, no changed execution semantics for the rest of the suite. The first placement was wrong and a real run said so. Draining in @Before still leaked, because Robolectric resets its shadow layer for method M before any of M+1 runs. The drain has to happen inside the causing test's own lifecycle, so it moved to @After across 78 files, plus two that build their own in-memory database and never touched the singleton. Bounded waits, added on review. A stale pool-size constant fails two ways: a grown pool under-drains and the leak returns looking like the original bug; a shrunk pool could never trip the barrier. Unbounded, the second case would HANG the suite - no report, no failing test name, and on CI the whole time budget burned before anyone learns anything. It now fails with an error naming the constant to fix. Verified across five clean full runs, test-results deleted each time: 2,744 tests, 0 failures, and 0 classes emitting the leak in system-err. The leak count is the assertion that matters. A green suite that still leaked would mean the casualty moved, not that the cause was fixed - which is exactly how this survived being waved off as a flake, by me, twice today. Not the permission, and not the files. ingested_files.driveFileId is a KEY, not an ADDRESS. stripAccountPrefix removes Drive's leading acc=N; on the way in, and its doc comment gives the right reason: that prefix is a positional local-account index, not part of the file's identity, and keeping it would make the key unstable across a second signed-in account. IngestScanner stores the stripped id at :183 and opens bytes with the full child.documentId at :192, so the live scan never round-trips through the stored form. The dry run did, handing a stripped id to buildDocumentUriUsingTree and producing a document id Drive does not recognise. Real values off the phone: stored doc=encoded=9SUKrD9cnjOCA5TdkI8TKpsIuHE3q5gJ... tree URI acc=1;doc=encoded=o_GGpalKBAfTlOkt93tJoIsI7YFN... reattachAccountPrefix is the documented inverse, sitting next to its counterpart so neither gets "simplified" without the other. The prefix is derived from the tree's own document id rather than stored, so a non-Drive provider that carries no prefix gets nothing fabricated, and an already-prefixed id is not double-prefixed. Both cases tested. The regression test asserts on the URI that gets built, and separately asserts the old direct-build path produces a different, wrong id - so it fails if the fix regresses rather than only if a read throws. ## How it got through, which is the part worth keeping The claim was "grepped the whole repo for the literal acc=, found zero producers of that prefix", tagged traced. True and irrelevant: the prefix is produced by Drive, not by this codebase, and the existence of stripAccountPrefix - a consumer that removes it - is itself proof the input carries it. Evidence gathered in the wrong direction and then labelled verified. The claim never landed in a comment or a ticket, so there was nothing in-repo to correct, but the shape is worth naming: an absence of producers inside one repo says nothing about what an external provider hands you. Suite: 2,740 tests, 0 failures. Owed: the on-device re-run. This is reasoned from a traced root cause plus a passing regression test, which is exactly the standard of evidence that produced the bug. Ticket 12's re-ingestion plan needs the three anchors back. The parsers were computing opening and closing balances for their own reconciliation and discarding them: BofaStatementParser, which handles the bulk of the eStmt PDFs, kept neither, and only Dbs and BofaCsv leaked one through the per-row balanceCents. Anchors are now a first-class result. DeterministicResult.Success carries StatementAnchors, and the four PDF/CSV bank parsers return ParsedStatement instead of a bare list. Per-row balanceCents keeps its old meaning and stops being mistaken for an anchor path: a running balance and the document's printed opening and closing figures are different things that coincide only at the ends, which is why this went unnoticed. ## The finding, and it is not the one expected **No bank format prints a single combined total.** Every one of them prints per-section figures instead: DBS separate withdrawal and deposit totals, BofA per-section payments/purchases/fees/interest, BofaCsv separate total credits and total debits. So statedTotalCents is NULL for every bank parser, honestly, and only LegionCsvStatementParser - the LLM-produced format LEGION defines - can supply all three. The old sum(amountCents) stand-in in the dry run made every file look complete. It is removed. What it was doing is the thing rule 6 forbids: sum(lines) presented as the document's stated total makes sum(lines) == stated_total an identity that cannot fail. So the honest picture is worse than the stand-in suggested and better than before the fix: BofaStatementParser goes from zero anchors to two real ones, and the rest go from one balance-derived value to two genuinely read ones. Two of three, not three. BofaCardCsvStatementParser stays at zero anchors and that is correct, not a gap - it is the rule-7 provisional path and its export states nothing to reconcile against, by design. Each parser test asserts the real printed opening and closing values and asserts statedTotalCents is null against a fixture whose lines sum to a nonzero amount, so reinstating the stand-in would fail. No fabricated "printed total differs from sum" fixture for the bank formats, because none of them prints a distinguishable total to build one from - said plainly rather than writing a test that cannot fail. The three-anchor CSV format, and a parse that refuses to be helpful
no ticket
ed5d7c5 · 7 files
Hard constraint C4: the format and its importer must work before the ledger cutover, and only then do the deterministic parsers come out. Neither existed. The server half was already done and proven - the RPC is applied and the 13-case corpus reports both implementations agree - so this is the format itself and the phone side that produces its payload. ## The format is a contract with the user's own LLM Not with a bank. That inverts the usual design pressure: it has to be simple enough that a person can describe it in a paragraph and an arbitrary model hits it first try. So it is two plain CSV tables, an anchor header and one row, then the lines, and there is deliberately NO quoting support - a quoting rule is one more thing for a model to get subtly wrong. Money is a bare signed integer of cents. No dollar sign, no commas, no decimal point, and anything else is REJECTED rather than coerced. That refusal is the point. The gate proves three printed numbers agree with each other; it cannot prove any one of them was read correctly, so a parser that helpfully strips a "$" is exactly how a misread digit enters the one place nothing downstream can catch it. Every cents field goes through a single regex or fails - no strip, no replace, no repair. Rows are tagged LLM_RECONCILED, never DETERMINISTIC. LEGION's own parse IS deterministic, but an LLM sat upstream, and provenance describes where data came from rather than what last touched it. A statement missing any one anchor cannot use the format at all and fails early, naming which anchor was absent. It falls to rule 7 provisional instead, which is where an unverifiable row belongs. ## The corpus now proves the real code path, not a lookalike The gate arithmetic came out into LedgerReconciliationCheck, one pure function mirroring commit_statement's SQL check for check and wording for wording. GateCorpusTest was reimplementing that arithmetic inline; it now calls the production function, so the corpus's own promise - "when the pre-check lands, plug in here" - is literally true. Kotlin production code, the corpus and the RPC agree by construction rather than by three hand-copied copies of one rule. That is better than the extra corpus cases I asked for, which would have padded coverage of shapes already covered while leaving the real function unproven. Recorded because the agent flagged the deviation rather than quietly taking it. The existing parsers are untouched and still dispatch. Ruling 3 retires them only once this path is proven end to end, and that removal is phase 6. 14 new parser cases, including each anchor missing separately, both mismatch shapes, dollar and comma amounts rejected rather than repaired, and two accounts sharing a last-4 kept apart by nickname - ruling 5 says that collision is real and the nickname is load-bearing. Suite: 2,715 tests, 0 failures. docs_check reports no drift. Widen the Google importer, so the metadata outlives Google
no ticket
6e36ef1 · 13 files
Hard constraint C3 from the migration path: widen the importer, run it unbounded, verify, and only THEN remove Google. The reason the order binds is that the class-schedule metadata lives ONLY in Google's event descriptions and is never stored, so cutting first deletes it for good. The importer handled none of description, location, allDay or the LEGION::v1 block, so nothing was ready to cut against. Now it does. description and location land in the existing engine fields, allDay and structuredMeta are new field defs (a FieldDef row, the engine's own zero-migration extension mechanism, not invented storage), and proseAfter is the counterpart to structuredBlock: the human-written text after the terminator, null and never "" when there is nothing to say - an empty string would later read as "the user wrote nothing", which is a claim the source never made. ## Unbounded is a different mode, not a wider window The windowed run's delete guard exists because a windowed query is narrower than what a differently-windowed prior run could have written, so an out-of-window row is not "gone from Google", merely out of scope. An unbounded run has no such gap: every google row is in scope by construction, so a row not re-seen really is gone. Reusing the guard would be reusing semantics built around a gap that does not exist. Added as a mode rather than a changed default, and the difference is tested both ways. Read in year-wide slices rather than one span, because CalendarProvider materializes a plain List with no paging contract. A multi-day event straddling a slice boundary is handled by writing new ids into the shared map immediately, so the second sighting updates rather than duplicates. ## The fields did not actually survive the trip, and that is the point Caught on review, after the work already looked complete and green: EventsReconcile hardcoded allDay = false for Dates events - it never read a field because Dates had no such field until this commit. So an all-day event imported true and uploaded false. Silent loss on the exact field just added, now read properly and asserted. structuredMeta reached nothing at all: no column, no DTO. The metadata rescued out of Google's description strings would have lived only in an engine field, and ruling 7 retires the engine. That defers the loss C3 exists to prevent rather than preventing it. Added structured_meta jsonb on public.events and carried it end to end. jsonb over text because a text blob is the "enforcement caps at whatever the client remembers" shape ruling 6 rejected. And the DTO carries it as JsonElement, not String: a String property serializes to Postgrest as a quoted JSON scalar, writing the whole object as one escaped string and destroying the indexability that was the reason for jsonb at all. Same fix SupabasePantryBackend already uses for the identical problem. EventReplica deliberately gets NO column and there is no v43. Nothing on the phone renders a LEGION::v1 block - the only live consumer reads straight off a Google description - so a Room migration would buy an unread column. The reasoning is on toReplica's doc comment so it is not silently "fixed" later without re-checking. Suite: 2,701 tests, 0 failures. 20260827000100 is NOT APPLIED. No CLI or credentials here, same as 54cdf5e. Owed with the fleet migrations. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

no ticket
fa58865 · 6 files
Fleet had no phone-side backend at all - vehicles and service_history have been sitting server-side since the 25th with nothing uploading to them, and drives since the 26th. This is the first wave, scoped to the three tables that are actually APPLIED. The four newest fleet tables (54cdf5e) are unapplied, so building against them would be building against a guess. ## Two identity shapes inside one aspect Every other aspect has been uniform. Fleet is not, and the difference is real rather than an oversight: vehicles and service_history ARE engine records, so they key on origin_guid from records.guid; drives never were engine records, so Drive.syncId was already the portable identity and there was nothing to invent. Documented in the code, because it reads like a mistake otherwise. ## The vehicle reference had to be composed, not read ServiceHistory names its vehicle by the engine record's Long id, Drive names it by the legacy obdMac string, and the server wants a uuid. The reconcile builds engine-id -> guid, obdMac -> guid and guid -> server uuid, then composes them. A row whose parent cannot resolve through that chain is SKIPPED and named in skippedUnresolvedVehicle - never uploaded with a guessed or empty parent, which would put a service record on the wrong car. ## Replicas: a real gap, reported rather than papered over drives reuses its own legacy table: the columns already match the server 1:1, it carries no local-only baggage, and it is append-only, so insert-if-absent needs no migration. vehicles and service_history CANNOT reuse theirs. The legacy Vehicle table is keyed on obdMac, which FleetRecordBridge's own doc says is not recoverable from the engine guid (a one-way nameUUIDFromBytes hash), and it carries a dozen local-only columns - persona, telemetry accumulators, archive state - that a server refill would have to blank. A genuine replica needs new Room tables the way EventReplica did for Notes. So this wave is upload-only for those two, and the gap is visible in the TYPE rather than hidden in a comment: VehicleReport and ServiceHistoryReport have no replicaCountAfter field at all. The migration was deliberately not written on an executing agent's own judgment. MaintenanceSchedule is out of scope: it has no origin_guid column in 20260826000100, so it was never part of this cutover. No live upsert or softDelete for vehicles/service_history either. No production caller exists this wave, and an uncalled, untested edit path is how a false success gets written. PantryBackend's minimal shape, not EventsBackend's fuller one. gallons stays Double? with no zero coercion end to end, with its own test: unknown fuel and no fuel are different facts and collapsing them makes MPG lie. provenance is never OBSERVED - that is a kind on service_history. Money stays Long cents. Suite: 2,690 tests, 0 failures. Nothing here has touched the live project. The reconcile cannot be diffed until Kevin applies 54cdf5e's migrations. The agenda shows an undated item as tomorrow, and says so in words
no ticket
c79da08 · 6 files
Ticket 01 ruling 2 has been decided since 2026-08-25 and nothing implemented it. Both agenda queries hard-filtered dueAt IS NOT NULL and toAgendaItems dropped null rows, so 53 of Kevin's 56 Notes items - 95% of everything he has authored in this aspect - never reached the agenda at all. That is a bug against the ruling, not a missing feature. All five clauses of the ruling, each load-bearing: INFERRED, never stored. Nothing is written; the date is synthesized per read. Storage keeps NULL, per ticket 07's own "what it does not license" and section 4 rule 5. TAGGED. AgendaItem.dueIsInferred is an explicit flag, not a sentinel date, so no caller has to infer the inference. SAID IN WORDS. An inferred item renders as "(showing tomorrow, no date set)", never a bare time that reads as stated. The spoken opener carries it too - clause 3 applies to speech, not just to a screen. ROLLS FORWARD. Computed from a nowMs parameter on every read and never cached, so it is always ahead and can never become yesterday. The parameter exists so tests can pin it rather than race the clock. NEVER NAGS, and this is the safety-relevant one. An inferred date must never fire an alarm: that would be the app asserting a deadline the user never set, which is rule 5 and fails the compulsion test's clause (a), since the anchor would not be a fact he could verify. The asymmetry is what makes that real - visible on the agenda, invisible to the alarm scheduler - and it is enforced STRUCTURALLY rather than by a filter. Inferred rows come from a separate DAO method that only windowed() calls; nextUnmuted and byId keep their untouched dueAt IS NOT NULL query and null guard, so an inferred row cannot reach the alarm path even if a future caller forgets it exists. A widened query with an OR would have made "never nags" depend on every caller remembering to filter it back out. The inferred instant is now + 24h rather than a calendar midnight. Accepted as a judgment call, not dictated by the ruling: it needs no timezone and is always ahead of now. Adding 24h lands on calendar tomorrow in every case except a near-midnight DST spring-forward, and since the rendered text never shows the date, the only thing affected is sort position. Six new tests, including the one that matters: an inferred row is excluded from nextUnmuted even when it would otherwise sort soonest. Suite: 2,676 tests, 0 failures. Derive the replica's local id instead of reminting it every reconcile
backend-erp 11
b17bc88 · 5 files
Ticket 11 grounding found a live defect, not a hazard to be careful of during the rewire. EventsReconcile.run deletes every replica row before refilling it, so EventReplicaDao.upsert's getByServerId branch always missed, every row took the insert path, and EVERY local id was reminted on EVERY reconcile. The hand-written id-preserving upsert was defeated by its only production caller; its doc comment described a guarantee the code did not deliver. That id is load-bearing: it is an AlarmManager PendingIntent request code, a notification id, and a soft foreign key from list_item_skips, workout_set_logs and muted_reminders. A reminted id orphans an armed alarm that can then never be cancelled, while the real one is silently dropped. Kevin's ruling: carry the engine id. events_replica.id is now DERIVED from the originating records.id via origin_guid rather than allocated by SQLite. A derived id cannot drift, so the defect dissolves rather than getting patched, and the cutover needs no rekey and no alarm re-arm. Two-pass refill, and the ordering is load-bearing. Rows with a derivable id are seated BEFORE any id is allocated. Without that, an ancestor-less row (created post-cutover on another surface, no origin_guid) refilling into the just-emptied table autoincrements from 1 and can take the very id a not-yet-processed migrated row must carry; the collision guard then correctly declines to clobber it and hands the migrated row a fresh id, which is the alarm orphaning the carry exists to prevent, reached by another route. An ancestor-less row has nothing pointing at its local id yet, so it is the one that can afford to move. upsert keeps three branches: an established id never moves, not even to a more correct carried one; an unoccupied carried id is honoured; else autoincrement. The collision guard stays as defence for callers other than the reconcile. Why no test caught it: the idempotence test asserted replicaCountAfter, never ids. Ticket 09's blind spot one layer out, and section 4 rule 6's shape - a check satisfiable without the thing it protects being present. The new stability test was confirmed RED against the unfixed code. Suite: 2,656 tests, 0 failures. compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey clean. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Instead the upload keys on the identity the data already has: every row being uploaded is an engine record, and MIGRATION_36_37 backfilled records.guid for every pre-existing row. Rows created after the cutover leave origin_guid NULL, and Postgres treats NULLs as distinct, so they never collide. This is not the engine shape leaking back in. Ruling 7 retires records, record_types, field_defs and the payload jsonb; a column recording where a row came from is the same kind of fact as provenance, and it outlives the engine. Parse-checked with tools/sql_check.py (10 migrations, 93 statements). NOT applied to the live project - that is a manual step, and sql_check green means the statements are well formed, never that they will apply cleanly. Phase 3: the read-state vocabulary, and a correction to what phase 3 is for
backend-erp 05
bea1cef · 4 files
ReadState is the pure, Compose-free piece: what a screen knows about its own last read, and the words it owes because of it. Nine tests, no Robolectric, following TodayGapResolvers, which is the in-house precedent for a builder that returns already-worded strings plus a severity flag so the composable picks a colour rather than re-deriving meaning from the string it is about to print. Kevin's two rulings are encoded in it. Fresh data says nothing, because a permanent "as of just now" trains the eye past exactly the line that matters once reads go remote. And a failure keeps the last good data on screen and says so, rather than blanking working figures over a transient blip. Ordering inside readStateLine is the design: a failure with no data ever loaded is worded differently from a failure with data, because "showing the last data read" would be a lie when there is nothing on screen; and a failure outranks staleness, since the age of the last successful read is misleading on its own. The staleness rule ships with tests but no live trigger, deliberately. Reads are still local and complete in milliseconds, so the app cannot reach it until phase 4. Shipping it tested-but-unreached is the considered alternative to shipping an untested half, which is exactly what the DatabaseSnapshot restore turned out to be on the one path nobody had run. Also corrects a claim I put in this ticket myself. I wrote that the three screens "have no loading state, so an empty screen and a not-yet-loaded screen are the same pixels", from a summary I did not check. All three already have loading booleans and screen-level indicators, and FleetUiState.odometerUnset even defaults to true so a not-yet-loaded state cannot open the miles axis. What is actually missing is narrower and worse: there is no error channel at all, no try/catch in any of the three load effects, so a Room or bundled-asset throw crashes rather than surfacing. Plus the ledger money tiles conflate "this month is reloading" with "no data", pantry has no reload path whatsoever, no screen records when its load completed, and none of the three has any screenshot coverage. And the two "as of" facts are separated in writing so nobody merges them later: AccountBalance.asOfMs is the statement document's date, ruling 9's is when this device last read its copy, and both can be true at once. Phase 2: the real ledger dedup, and a schema bug it exposed
no ticket
07f77f3 · 3 files
Replaces the placeholder tuple match with a faithful port of LedgerDedup.resolveDedup: two passes over a shared, depleting credit pool. Exact strict-key matches first with no window condition, then loose matches with the description dropped, permitted only inside dates another committed statement already enumerated completely. Transcribed as a loop rather than expressed as an anti-join. A set-based version is derivable but only provably equivalent after working the arithmetic; a faithful loop that is obviously right beats a clever join that is probably right when the question is whether money gets counted twice. Three properties are load-bearing and each has a Kotlin test pinning it. Pass one runs completely before pass two, so a row that can be matched precisely never spends a loose credit another row needs. Both passes decrement the same pool, so one committed row absorbs exactly one incoming row and never two. And incoming is never deduplicated against itself, because two identical lines in one statement are two genuine purchases; collapsing them is the original bug the function exists to fix. The port exposed a real problem in my own schema rather than in the Kotlin. LedgerAccountIdentity is emphatic that sameCard's last-four suffix match must never be folded into the dedup key, since a checking account ending in the same four digits would absorb a card's rows. Ticket 03 ruling 5 then made the stored identity last-four plus nickname, so keying dedup on account_last4 alone would have reintroduced exactly that bug through the schema instead of the predicate. The key is now the pair, which restores plain equality on a full identity. The nickname is load-bearing, not a label. Windows derive their bounds from the actual first and last transaction dates rather than the printed period, because a printed period can run past the last transaction and claiming completeness over that tail would be unsupported. Derived rather than stored so it cannot drift from the rows. One accepted divergence is documented in place: Kotlin's uppercase is Locale.ROOT with full Unicode mapping, Postgres upper is collation-driven and does not expand one-to-many. For ASCII bank descriptions it never bites, and the failure direction is known - a divergence causes a false non-match, which double-counts. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Phase 2: the commit RPC, with the gate and rule 7 in one transaction

39a44c3 · 2 files
The reconciliation gate, server side. Everything IngestPipeline.commit does inside one db.withTransaction now happens inside one PostgREST request, which is one Postgres transaction. One deliberate deviation from ticket 03's literal wording, stated at the top of the file rather than buried. The ticket says the RPC raises on a gate mismatch. Taken literally that is wrong: a raise rolls back everything including the quarantine record, so the file would return on the next scan with no memory of why it failed, forever. A gate failure is an outcome, not an exception, and the Kotlin version already treats it that way. It returns QUARANTINED having written exactly one file-status row and zero lines, which is what "nothing partial is ever written" actually prohibits: partial DATA, never the record that a document was rejected. Raise is reserved for genuinely exceptional states. Rule 6 runs FIRST, before any arithmetic, and the ordering is the point. A zero-line extraction sails through every anchor whenever the statement's own figures happen to be zero, because the sum of no rows is zero and a month with no movement has closing equal to opening. That is not hypothetical; it is how BofA's card statement passed with four silently dropped interest rows, and it only held because interest was zero that month. Rule 7 supersession runs before the dedup read, carrying all three load-bearing properties: a provisional file never supersedes anything including a prior import of itself, the ordering stops verified rows being discarded as duplicates of the provisional ones they replace, and it is in the same transaction by construction. sameCard becomes the last-four match, and its collision weakness carries over unchanged, which is what the nickname is for. Idempotency is keyed on the content hash, so a repeat call returns ALREADY_COMMITTED having written nothing. That is what lets the phone retry a lost ack instead of narrating a state CANNOT_CLAUSE has no vocabulary for. Dedup is deliberately incomplete rather than quietly partial: the tuple match is implemented, the overlapping-window restatement pass that distinguishes a real duplicate from a bank restating a period is not, and the comment says so and says it is owed before the phase 4 ledger cutover. The intra-file behaviour is also spelled out rather than left to be discovered. Not verified: no Postgres has run any of this. pglast parses the statements but plpgsql bodies are opaque to it, so every function body here is unproven. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Phase 2: all six aspects as typed tables, gated ones header-plus-lines
no ticket
3a5a6f9 · 4 files
Ten tables across three migrations, 58 statements, all parsing against Postgres's own grammar. The gated aspects get the shape Kevin ruled: a header carrying the anchors, with lines foreign-keyed to it. That is not a modelling preference. The gate's claim is that a set of lines reconciles against something the document stated, so making the anchor a header row the lines reference means a line cannot exist without the anchor it was checked against. "Nothing partial is ever written" stops being a property the commit code remembers and becomes one the database will not allow to be violated. Two constraints encode rule 7 rather than describing it. statements requires all three anchors NOT NULL, because a document that cannot state them cannot use the format at all. And ledger_transactions.statement_id is nullable precisely so a provisional row can exist without a header, with a CHECK tying the two together: reconciled rows must have one, provisional rows must not. The schema says in the only language it has that a provisional row was never checked against anything. Reversal columns carry the SAP document principle, and there is deliberately no reversed_by anywhere, because setting one would mean updating an immutable row. The Notes-into-Dates merge lands as one events table. Twenty-one Item fields and seven Event fields become one shape with nothing dropped, and event_skips carries over list_item_skips for the reason it existed before: occurrences are computed from the recurrence rule and never stored, so a skip has nowhere else to live. This is the only aspect with no legacy table to retreat to, which is why the merge happens here rather than twice. Fleet is where ADR 0039 pays for itself most visibly. "You may not delete a vehicle that still has service history" was a rule RecordStore enforced in Kotlin on every caller's behalf; it is now ON DELETE RESTRICT, which no future consumer can route around. Not verified: nothing has been applied. pglast validates statement structure but not plpgsql bodies, so the immutability trigger's body is still unproven, and no CHECK constraint has ever rejected anything. Phase 2: schema conventions, and a parser so the SQL is not written blind
no ticket
71e42b2 · 3 files
The shared vocabulary every aspect table will follow: the provenance type, the immutability rule for gated data, updated_at for authored data, the household RLS macro, and the server-side ingested_files whose content hash is the commit RPC's idempotency key. Two design points are worth reading rather than skimming. Immutability and rule 7 appeared to collide: gated rows are append-only, but rule 7 deletes superseded provisional rows. The resolution is principled rather than a carve-out. Immutability protects rows asserted as FACT, and rule 7's own definition of a provisional row is that it is never asserted as fact and is transient. A row that was never a claim cannot be falsified by withdrawing it. So the trigger blocks every update, and blocks deletes except on UNRECONCILED. Freezing provisional rows instead would stop rule 7 running at all. There is deliberately no reversed_by column. Setting one would require updating an immutable row, which is the thing being forbidden. A reversal carries reversal_of, and "is this reversed" is a lookup rather than stored state. The RLS macro grants table privileges explicitly rather than leaning on Supabase's project defaults. If those defaults were ever altered, the tables would be unreadable and RLS would look like the culprit. tools/sql_check.py parses every migration through pglast, which wraps libpg_query, Postgres's own grammar. This matters because nothing on this machine can run Postgres: no psql, no Docker. Both migrations parse, 25 statements. Its docstring is explicit about what it cannot catch, because a check that overstates itself is worse than none: plpgsql function bodies are opaque string literals to the outer grammar and are only parsed by Postgres at execution, and nothing semantic is verified. Green means well formed, never "will apply". Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ticket 03's "engine retirement before or with the RPC" does not mean deleting 15,885 lines up front - the server schema is typed from day one so the RPC is never built against the generic shape, while the phone's engine retires per aspect. And legacy-table drops no longer mean what they did, because ruling 7 sends the phone back to those very tables; they are the destination, not drop candidates. Ticket 03 resolved: one idempotent RPC, and the statement parsers retire
backend-erp 01backend-erp 03backend-erp 05
293e4d3 · 10 files
Eight rulings. Two of them change things outside this ticket. The commit becomes a single Supabase RPC, idempotent on the file's content hash. That idempotency is not a nicety: ticket 01's ruling 8 removed the offline queue, so a network death after Postgres commits but before the ack leaves the phone unable to tell success from failure, and AriaBrain's CANNOT_CLAUSE is binary - a tool result is successful or it is nothing, with no vocabulary for "unknown". Making the RPC a successful no-op on repeat means the phone retries until the answer is definitive instead of narrating a state it cannot describe honestly. Gate arithmetic runs server-side with the phone pre-checking, which buys a fast local fail at the cost of two implementations that must not drift. The larger change is Kevin's own proposal: the deterministic statement parsers retire. A statement goes through the user's own LLM, which masks sensitive data and emits a CSV in a format LEGION defines. That kills PdfBox and with it the Deno problem, covers every bank rather than only DBS and BofA, and puts masking before upload, which matters more now the truth lives in a cloud Postgres. It amends CLAUDE.md section 4 rule 1, and the amendment is written in there, marked decided-but-not-built so nobody reads the parsers as already gone. The gate gets stronger to pay for it. An LLM-produced CSV has its lines and its total from one nondeterministic process, so a single anchor could be satisfied by a hallucination that hallucinated its own total to match - rule 6's failure shape in a new place. The format therefore demands three separately printed anchors, and a statement carrying fewer falls to rule 7 provisional instead. Ticket 01's ruling 10 is amended the same day: photo files may leave the device, to a private bucket in the household's own project, because Edge-Function receipt vision cannot work otherwise. The other three stay phone-only. Three pre-existing defects are filed on the ticket rather than lost, the sharpest being that the four tests covering rule-7 supersession have not touched production code since cutover 3. That lowers the Room-side cost of ruling 7 substantially; it lowers neither the Postgres DDL work nor the Item-into-Event merge. It also sets the shape: reconcile-and-repoint per aspect, engine records staying truth until each diff comes back clean. The legacy tables are about a day stale for whatever cut over on 08-24, so a blind switch back would lose that day. Ticket 05 now owns three retirements and their order. Ticket 01 keeps the rulings and the measurements; 05 keeps the sequencing. Nothing is deleted until it says so. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

MUST-FIX: reconcileSupersededProvisional trashed any active engine UNRECONCILED row whose guid was missing from legacy allSyncIds(). Post- cutover, IngestPipeline.commit/LedgerController.logPendingTransaction create brand-new engine UNRECONCILED rows whose guid never touched the legacy table - always missing by construction. A driver importing a CSV or voice-logging a pending transaction on first launch, before the fire-and-forget catchUpOnce coroutine finishes, would have that legitimate row silently trashed. Fixed with a persisted migrated-guid set (migrated_guids_v1): copyLedgerIfNeeded records every guid it confirms as legacy-derived, and reconcileSupersededProvisional gates on membership in that set before ever checking legacy presence. A createdAt-cutoff was considered and rejected: both the copier and IngestPipeline's own create call pass now = txn.txnDate to RecordStore.create, so createdAt reflects the transaction's own date for both migrated and live rows, never wall-clock insert time - a timestamp comparison would have been silently wrong on real data. New tests: catchUpOnce never trashes an engine-native row whose guid was never in the legacy table, even if created before reconcile runs (the race itself); catchUpOnce still trashes a genuinely migrated row once its legacy backing disappears, proving the new gate isn't overbroad (positive control). SHOULD-FIX: RecordStore._afterWrite.tryEmit fires inside the caller's withTransaction. Traced rather than changed - the only production subscriber always routes through MirrorSync.scheduleExport(), which delays 5 seconds and reads fresh via DAO calls at read time, well past any ledger/pantry multi-row transaction's settle time, and independent of that margin Room's own transactional isolation means a reader outside a transaction cannot observe its uncommitted writes. Documented in RecordStore.kt's afterWrite doc comment. No test: a genuine cross-connection commit/rollback race is not something Robolectric's single-process SQLite harness can be trusted to reproduce meaningfully. Suite green both key ways. voice_guide.py exit 0.

Fix row/col swap at the move-commit call site; extract pointer-to-cell mapping
no ticket
ac3f032 · 3 files
Sixth feel-test pass, Kevin reproduced over adb with screenshots: dragging ANY full-width card any distance in any direction always committed at row 0, col 0. ROOT CAUSE, exact location: DeckGrid.kt's onMoveDragEnd computed the commit candidate with two adjacent, UNNAMED run { } blocks passed positionally into GridEngine.clampMoveTarget(item, targetRow, targetCol, columnCount). The FIRST block - landing in the targetRow slot - computed a COLUMN value (built from colPitchPx/originCol/accumPx.x). The SECOND block - landing in targetCol - computed a ROW value (built from rowPitchPx/originRow/accumPx.y). Row and column were transposed at that one call site. Why it always read as (0,0): clampMoveTarget clamps targetCol into [0, columnCount - colSpan]. For a FULL-width card that range is exactly [0, 0], so whatever value the swap put in the targetCol slot clamped to 0 regardless of magnitude - and the swap put the near-zero column value (unchanged from originCol, since every reproduction was a vertical-only drag on a card already at column 0) into targetRow, which floors at 0 and stayed ~0. Two independent near-misses that both happened to land on 0 for every widget in the reproduction, since all of them are full-width and start at column 0. The live preview computation a few lines above (the drag's own on-screen ghost outline) did the identical arithmetic CORRECTLY, named its results candidateRow/candidateCol, and passed them in the right order - only the commit path, which duplicated the arithmetic inline instead of reusing one implementation, got the order wrong. That is why the preview outline looked right during the drag while the drop still reverted: two different, divergent computations of the same value. FIX, per the brief's three-part demand: 1. Root cause found and fixed at the exact line (the onMoveDragEnd call site's two run { } blocks, now replaced with a single named, correctly-ordered destructure). 2. JVM test added that would have caught it: GridGestureTest."dragging DOWN increases row, column unchanged - the exact shape that broke" reproduces the precise symptom shape (vertical- only drag, origin column 0) and asserts row and column land independently, never conflated. 3. The pointer-to-cell mapping is now its OWN pure function, GridGesture.candidateCell(originRow, originCol, accumPxX, accumPxY, colPitchPx, rowPitchPx) -> Pair<row, col>, in GridModel.kt (zero Compose imports, same as every other function in that file). Both the live preview and the commit call this SAME function now - there is exactly one implementation of this arithmetic left anywhere, so there is nothing left to diverge. GridGestureTest covers up/down/left/right/diagonal, sub-cell jitter that stays inside a pitch band (must not move), sub-cell jitter that crosses a boundary (must move), row floored at 0, column deliberately NOT floored (clamping is the caller's job), non-zero origin, and an explicit "row from Y, col from X, never swapped" case. This is the third consecutive pass to ship a gesture-math bug invisible to the JVM suite because the arithmetic lived inline in Compose code - it now has direct coverage, leaving only pointer EVENT PLUMBING (detectDragGestures wiring, state threading) as the honest remainder no JVM test can reach. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.
Fix normalize-on-every-recomposition, half-width chip overlap, content clipping
no ticket
088a01f · 4 files
Fifth feel-test pass, Kevin plus a screenshot, three defects: 1. DROP DOES NOT STICK IN EMPTY SPACE. Confirmed cause: baseItems was remember(items.toList(), columnCount) { GridEngine.normalize(items, columnCount) }. Fixing the fourth-pass bug (remember never invalidating) made baseItems recompute for real on every content change for the first time - which made GridEngine.normalize's own unconditional compact() visible for the first time too. normalize is correct and intentional for untrusted FIRST input (a raw widget_instances read, hand-typed fixtures) but was never meant to run on an already-committed, already-valid layout - compact() with no pinned id pulls a deliberately-gapped layout upward on every single call, so every commit's own recomposition immediately re-compacted the card the user just placed in an empty space. JVM test written FIRST, documents the exact mechanism: GridEngineTest."normalize does NOT round-trip a valid gapped layout untouched" - a two-item collision-free layout with a deliberate gap, run through normalize, is NOT bit-identical (the gapped item gets pulled up). This test passes against the unmodified GridEngine (normalize's own behavior was never the bug - it is correct for what it is; calling it repeatedly was the bug). Traced end to end: DeckGrid.kt's baseItems val, computed every recomposition once the fourth-pass fix made the remember key real, called GridEngine.normalize -> compact(settled, pinnedId = null) -> pulled every gapped item to the top of its column. That is the exact function moving the card. Fix: normalize now runs EXACTLY ONCE per DeckGrid instance (the accepted "one-shot flag" idiom - a remembered boolean flips true-to-false on the very first composition and never again). Every recomposition after that trusts `items` verbatim, no processing at all - a value that already round-tripped through this component's own commit path (displaceForPlacement, clampMoveTarget, clampResizeTarget) is already valid, and reprocessing it is exactly what silently relocated the user's own placement. 2. HALF-WIDTH CHROME BROKEN (screenshot: "LOG A DRIVE // QU" truncated by the opaque remove chip drawn on top, not by ellipsis). The chip and resize handle are drawn by DeckGrid.kt's GridCellChrome, layered on top of the caller's own DeckPane - DeckPane has no idea either exists, so its pill's own ellipsis clamp (paneWidth - 16dp) was computed against the FULL card width, with no awareness that a 28dp opaque chip sits on top of the last ~30-40dp of it. On a half-width card with a two-clause title, the pill legitimately rendered text (with its own ellipsis) reaching into the chip's zone, and the chip visually swallowed the ellipsis dots along with the last few characters. Fixed by reserving a CHIP_CLEARANCE (36dp) off the trailing edge of `content()` itself, edit mode only - so DeckPane's own ellipsis point, and any right-reaching content inside it (DeckButton's fill width), naturally stop clear of where the chip and handle actually sit. Does not touch DeckPane (shared production component used across many existing screens) at all. 3. CONTENT CLIPPING (agenda card's third row sliced mid-glyph at the card's bottom edge). Two-part fix: (a) DeckGrid's own per-cell Box now carries Modifier.clipToBounds() as a structural, defensive guarantee - any widget whose content overflows its assigned rowSpan now cuts cleanly at the card's own boundary instead of bleeding a half-visible glyph past it; (b) the actual overflowing mocks are fixed at the source - PrototypeGrid.kt's initialGridItems now assigns AGENDA and RECORD_LIST kinds (both render three DeckRows, 144dp, plus header/padding chrome) two rows tall instead of one, which comfortably fits all three rows without needing the clip at all in practice. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.
Fix root cause of every drop reverting: remember(mutatedList) never invalidates
no ticket
a17af39 · 2 files
Fourth feel-test verdict: "doesnt commit, i drop card to new position but it snaps back to old position." ROOT CAUSE (confirmed): baseItems was remember(items, columnCount) { GridEngine.normalize(items, columnCount) }, keyed directly on items. The harness's items is a SnapshotStateList mutated IN PLACE (clear() + addAll(), never replaced with a new instance). remember's change-check compares the new key against the previously stored key via equals() - since both are literally the SAME mutated object, the comparison degenerates to x.equals(x), which is trivially true regardless of what the list now holds. baseItems froze at whatever it computed on DeckGrid's very first composition and never recomputed again: every card rendered its pre-drag position forever, and every settle animation's target was that same frozen position. onLayoutChange correctly updated the caller's own state the whole time - DeckGrid's own baseItems just never noticed. Coordinator's hypothesis (a self-overlap flaw in GridEngine.displaceForPlacement, the mover's own old position counting as an obstacle to itself) was checked FIRST via a new GridEngineTest case - "a short move whose candidate overlaps the mover's OWN old cells still commits, mover excluded" - and PASSES against the existing code, disproving it at the GridEngine layer: others already filters it.id != candidate.id before any collision check runs. The bug lived entirely in DeckGrid.kt's own composition, not in the pure model - stated plainly per the Compose-plumbing precedent from the first feel-test pass's resize-commit bug. Fix: key on items.toList() instead of items - a genuinely new immutable copy taken fresh every recomposition, so remember's equals check compares real structural List content against a frozen snapshot from last time, never an object against itself. Fixes move AND resize identically, since both share the same baseItems value - no separate resize-specific flaw existed. Deferred polish added in the same pass: displaced occupants now animate to their new cells with the same 200ms settle the actively dragged/resized card gets, instead of jumping. displacementSettle is a map keyed by id (an Animatable per currently-settling occupant) rather than a single shared Animatable, since one drop's knock-on chain can displace more than one occupant at once; startDisplacementSettles is called from both onMoveDragEnd and onResizeDragEnd right after a valid commit, guarding against a stale coroutine clobbering a newer settle for the same id. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.
Displace, not reject: occupied targets make room instead of refusing
no ticket
334e1e6 · 3 files
Fourth feel-test verdict: 'feels better. but it doesnt replace or move the items in the grid up if something is already there.' Snap model stays; occupied-target behavior changes from REJECT to DISPLACE. 1. New GridEngine.displaceForPlacement(items, candidate, columnCount): the candidate is always accepted exactly as proposed, and whatever it overlaps relocates to the nearest free space, searching upward first (closest row above, then columns left to right), then downward (candidate's own row and below) when upward is exhausted. Only actual overlapped occupants (plus any dependent chain through processing order) move; anything the candidate and its chain never touched stays bit-identical. Returns null only when genuinely impossible - a displaced occupant's own colSpan wider than columnCount (row search is unbounded, column width is not) or the candidate itself out of bounds. 2. DeckGrid.kt's drag/resize commit path now calls displaceForPlacement instead of commitIfValid. overlapsAny/commitIfValid (the second generation's outright-reject pair) are kept, doc-marked unused by the interactive path - same posture as moveTo/resize/resolveCollisions/ compact from the earlier rework. 3. Preview honesty: while hovering a spot that would displace, every occupant that would actually move is shown as a chrome-dim ghost outline at its would-be new cell, computed from the SAME displaceForPlacement call the eventual commit uses, so the drop can never differ from what was previewed. The candidate's own outline stays chrome-text (valid) or quarantine (the null/impossible case) - that null case is now the ONLY thing that still triggers the error-tone-and-animate-home rejection. 4. Out-of-bounds candidate clamping is unchanged (clampMoveTarget/ clampResizeTarget still run before displaceForPlacement). 5. GridEngineTest: 12 new displaceForPlacement cases - no-op when nothing overlaps, single occupant moved to the nearest free row above, moves down when upward is exhausted, finds a free column at the same row before changing rows, two simultaneously-colliding occupants chained through processing order, a defensive case for the (provably unreachable under this construction, kept as a safety net) knock-on requeue branch, null on an occupant whose own colSpan cannot fit any column, null on an out-of-bounds candidate, no-op-wrapped-non-null on an unknown id, and bit-identical untouched items. Known scope cut, stated rather than hidden: displaced OTHER occupants land at their new cell without their own settle animation - only the actively dragged/resized card gets one, carried over from the prior pass. Animating every knock-on occupant simultaneously is a larger change than this rework; flagged as follow-up polish. compileDebugKotlin, testDebugUnitTest (both key ways), assembleDebug all green.

It gates both the immediate and the delayed reconnect, and the delayed one re-checks after its delay because the delay can itself carry the last interaction out of the window. It composes with the existing prewarm-failure backoff rather than replacing it: a dead key and an idle app are different failures wanting different guards. The three cold paths are untouched, so a tap, a wake word and a proactive raise all still connect from a fully closed socket. The raise path is traced rather than tested, and says so: requestSpeak with no session falls to startProactive, which builds a session and speaks on Connected. A silent raise would be a worse bug than the churn, which is why it was checked rather than assumed. The trade is real and is in the code comments: the first thing said after a long idle pays a cold connect, about a second more than warm, once per idle stretch instead of 565 times a day. The 10 minute window is GUESSED. It says so where it is defined. Tool descriptions were deliberately not trimmed, though control_music and manage_item are the fattest things in the payload. The doctrine the recommender will reason from, and two contested numbers
goal-plans 01goal-plans 02
a1b9790 · 7 files
goal-plans ticket 01. Position stands, meta-analyses and government guidance only - findings with per-claim citations, plus the draft playbook ticket 02 will lift into a PrimingTopic. TWO NUMBERS ARE GENUINELY CONTESTED, AND NEITHER IS A ROUNDING DETAIL The ISSN's 2.3-3.1 g/kg protein figure for hypocaloric periods traces back to a source that states it per kg of LEAN mass, inside a document whose other positions use total bodyweight. For a lean person the two are close. At ~35% body fat they differ by about a third - the gap between a sane target and an unreachable one. And 0.5-1.0% bodyweight per week is the recommended rate, but the evidence for its top end comes from lean, resistance-trained athletes. Whether someone carrying more fat can safely lose faster is not established. Settled decision 5 said say-it-once rather than hedge forever. These two are the exception: contested in the literature rather than merely estimated, so the playbook states the disagreement instead of picking a side. TWO THINGS IT REFUSES TO INVENT There is no established point where added volume reverses hypertrophy - the meta-regressions show flattening, not a downturn. Any specific "junk volume" number is secondary-source folklore and the playbook says not to invent one. And kettlebells have never been equated against barbell training for hypertrophy. Kevin's own example turns out to have the weakest evidence base of anything asked about, so the playbook recommends them as reasonable and says plainly that no meta-analysis backs the equivalence. The substitution gaps - loaded knee flexion, vertical pull without an anchor, heavy hinge past the point bodyweight reaches failure inside thirty reps - are reasoned from the load-independence precondition rather than tested directly, and are tagged that way in both documents. A recommender claiming a home gym has no gaps would be overclaiming. The kidney boundary is the sharpest refusal: CKD guidance is 0.55-0.80 g/kg/day, directly contradicting every protein recommendation in the doctrine. That is why it must be a refusal and a referral rather than a quietly halved number. Also updates L32. Worktree isolation was tried per that lesson's own rule and FAILED: a fresh worktree has no local.properties, that file is gitignored, and it holds sdk.dir - so neither agent could run gradle at all, and both stalled fighting it. Their code was fine and dropped straight into the main tree. Copy local.properties into any worktree before dispatching an agent that must build. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

That is the difference between this and the AirNow client we deliberately did not write, and it paid for itself four times: USGS puts coordinates as [lon, lat, depth] and its free-text "place" is not reliable for a consistent spoken distance, so bearing and distance are computed from geometry rather than read from prose. Geocoder.adminArea returns "Texas" while FEMA and FBI both filter on "TX", and Android has no API for that conversion. Hence UsStates.kt. Asked that, it says so and offers the historical figure instead. A named place matching no agency returns null rather than silently answering about the nearest one - answering about the wrong jurisdiction is worse than not answering. HONEST SIMPLIFICATIONS, RECORDED FEMA is filtered by state, not county; resolving a county to FEMA's numeric fipsCountyCode needs a table this ticket did not scope. The output names the actual designatedArea, so nothing claims more locality than it has. AIR is deliberately absent and commented as such - AirNow is blocked on ticket 10's login visit. Ticket 05 of the location-intelligence map. Real OS geofences replace the raw distance math on GPS polls, which is what makes place reminders fire when the app is closed rather than depending on a poll happening to land near the place. Nearest-80 of Android's 100 cap, re-registered on the existing 20s arrival poll rather than a second timer, and re-registered from BootReceiver because geofences do not survive a reboot. THE BEST PART WAS NOT ASKED FOR Arrival handling was private inside AriaForegroundService. It is now ArrivalController.onArrived, so the geofence receiver and the GPS poll call ONE function instead of two copies that would have drifted. Any future arrival signal calls that. A FORK THE BUILD SURFACED RATHER THAN IMPROVISED Both signals now converge on that one handler with no debounce - and on a real arrival both will usually fire, seconds apart. That is the same reminder read out twice for one arrival. The build flagged it and stopped, which was right. Resolved with claimAnnouncement(place, now): check-and-claim in ONE step, because the geofence runs on a broadcast thread and the poll on the service scope, and a separate check-then-stamp would let both pass before either stamped. Five tests, including that a second announcement re-arms the window instead of leaving it open. AND A BUG FOUND WHILE IN THERE The raise used ruleId "place_arrival" for every place, so brushing off the reminder at the gym would have silenced arrivals at work and home for a day. Now per-place. That is the second time today a shared ruleId has been the wrong default - reminder_due was the first - so the pattern is worth naming: a rule id that is not per-subject is the exception, not the norm. The old GPS-poll path is KEPT deliberately. It is the fallback for anyone on foreground-only location, and removing it here would make place reminders worse for them. Retiring it belongs to a later ticket, once geofences are proven on the phone. play-services-location is a new dependency; play-services-auth was Drive-only. Owed on the phone, and the reboot case is the one the ticket itself named as most likely to be quietly broken: BootReceiver's call will usually no-op, since there is no GPS fix in the first milliseconds after boot, and the real re-arm comes moments later from the first poll. Spotify took focus outright. The trap is one line. duckNow() opens with `if (ducked) return`, and nothing cleared `ducked` on a focus loss, because the focus listener was diagnostic only. So the flag stayed true while the app no longer HELD focus, every later turn short-circuited, and focus was never re-requested for the rest of the session. The AudioTrack kept being written to and the system kept it inaudible. Subtitles kept working because output transcription arrives over the socket and never touches the audio path. That is why this presented as "it works but is silent" instead of as a failure, why nothing errored anywhere, and why it looked intermittent - it needs Spotify to grab focus once, then persists. The fix is that the listener now clears `ducked` on LOSS, LOSS_TRANSIENT and LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK. Nothing else. It deliberately does not pause playback, alter capture, or grab focus back - taking focus from whatever just claimed it is how two apps fight over a car stereo. Losing focus is normal; never noticing was the bug. Worth recording why this was findable at all. That listener was added on 2026-08-17 as instrumentation, with a comment saying reacting before a real log pull "would be exactly the kind of guess this file's own delicacy warns against". Without it there would have been no onAudioFocusChange line to find and this stays a mystery about the car stereo. The instrumentation went in before the fix was justified, and the fix waited for its evidence. Both halves mattered. The wake word being weak is filed separately as its own ticket with no diagnosis, because it has none yet - three candidate causes that are three different bugs. An output fix must not be credited with an input improvement it did not make. Also explains the sitrep report: the build on his phone predated the sitrep entirely, so there was no get_sitrep tool and the model improvised from location and weather. Current build now installed and hash-verified. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

TomTom: no storage at all, no spoken credit, and a licence read knowingly
location-intelligence 06location-intelligence 07location-intelligence 09
503b2fb · 18 files
The caching research came back bigger than the question it was asked. STORAGE IS ZERO, not "until we check" Routing returns Cache-Control: no-cache with no max-age. Clause 11.4 permits caching only up to "the maximum age indicated in such cache control headers", and nothing is indicated - so the carve-out permits zero. "Results" covers a travel-time integer exactly as it covers a polyline; there is no derived-number allowance of the kind Google and HERE grant. On-device is not a loophole: 11.4.1 regulates caching "in clients" and the phone IS the client. Clause 11.6.1 independently forbids creating "any secondary or derived database" from Results, which is what a table of accumulated ETAs is. That is a second, independent reason decision 15 chose a global prep buffer - the history a learned buffer would need cannot legally exist. THE LICENCE QUESTION I DID NOT ASK The free key licenses "internal evaluation and testing by you", and the paid tier is scoped to apps with "Asset Management Functionality" licensed to end users. LEGION is neither. Kevin read the former as covering a sideloaded personal build with one developer and one user - recorded as decision 17, a deliberate reading of an ambiguous term rather than something missed. Stated with its uncertainty intact: the pricing page advertises the free tier without ever calling it Evaluation Use, and neither document maps the two onto each other. Failure mode is a revoked key, never a bill - there is no card. ATTRIBUTION DROPPED, against my recommendation Kevin's call, decision 19. I argued for keeping "per TomTom" because decision 6 exists so a third-party claim never sounds like LEGION's own. The cost is stated once on the map and not re-litigated. The counter-argument is real: 17.3 wants the Copyright API and a LOGO for Routing results, a voice surface cannot render one, so no spoken phrasing was ever compliant. Decision 19 NARROWS decision 6 rather than reversing it - NWS, USGS, NIFC, AirNow, FEMA and FBI results are still always attributed. Decision 4's row now points at its own supersessions instead of contradicting them. Also filed ticket 09 as KIV: the rest of the TomTom surface area. Kevin's key enables reverse geocoding, places search, traffic incidents, reachable range, snap-to-roads and more. Inventoried with a view on which are plausible for a voice assistant and which are not - and noting that TomTom's own Geofencing API is already decided against, because the Android OS one is free, on-device and needs no round trip. It is the whole point of the map and it was invisible in ticket 15. Now ticket 01, blocking almost everything. Alert repetition. An NWS warning stays active for an hour, so without a rule it re-announces every cycle. Once per stable alert id, ever - and an upgrade from watch to warning is a new id, so it does speak. Cadence. 15 minutes, and only when location changed meaningfully. NWS sanctions 30 seconds; that is their limit, not a sensible rate for a phone on a desk. Silence at the garage. He chose to note it and build anyway, against my recommendation. Written into decision 16 and into ticket 04 in those words: the first real tornado warning is also the first test of whether delivery works at all. Nobody should later mistake silence for "no warnings". TWO RESEARCH TICKETS FIRED AT CHARTING TIME AirNow's lat/lon endpoints sit under a heading reading "Web Services that will be retired in the fall of 2026", weeks away - writing that client now is throwaway work. And TomTom's caching clause is unverified, which blocks STORING an ETA rather than computing one. THE KEY Kevin pasted his TomTom key. Close enough that assuming success would be the exact kind of guess this codebase keeps getting burned by, so CallAudioRoute asks and then checks what the route actually is, and names what it landed on instead when it did not move - a Bluetooth headset or the car legitimately winning is the likely case in Kevin's own use. The gap is stated rather than hidden: the readback is immediate, so a dialer that re-routes a second later is not caught. Cost is bounded - he hears the wrong speaker and says so - and polling audio state for seconds while he is trying to talk to someone is worse. A refused speaker does NOT make the answer a failure. The call is connected either way, and the two are reported as separate facts; success=false there would have the assistant say it could not answer a call it had just answered. Two tests pin that, including that a plain answer says nothing about the route at all. setCommunicationDevice on API 31+, the deprecated isSpeakerphoneOn below it. Say who is calling, and answer or decline it by voice
no ticket

Kevin: "i wanna know whos calling. right now only announces that theres a call. can i also pick it up or decline via voice?" Both yes. Three permissions, each verified against AOSP rather than assumed. WHY IT ONLY EVER SAID "A CALL" Not an oversight - the old code documented the limit and worked around it. TelephonyRegistry computes `r.canReadCallLog() ? phoneNumber : ""` on every callback delivery, so an app without READ_CALL_LOG is handed an EMPTY STRING, not null. LEGION held READ_PHONE_STATE only, so a generic line was the honest answer available. Now declared: READ_CALL_LOG (the only thing that delivers the number), READ_CONTACTS (number to name via PhoneLookup), ANSWER_PHONE_CALLS (an ordinary dangerous permission - TelecomServiceImpl checks it and its app-op and nothing else, so no dialer role is needed). READ_CALL_LOG is hard-restricted and would block a Play listing. LEGION is sideloaded and never listed, and adb install allowlists it by default. Written into the manifest so the day that changes, the constraint is already there. DO NOT migrate to TelephonyCallback.CallStateListener. Its onCallStateChanged has no number parameter at all - AOSP's dispatch comment says "The new callback does NOT provide the phone number" - so modernising off the deprecated PhoneStateListener would silently delete this feature. Said in the manifest and on the class. FOUR OUTCOMES, NONE OF THEM A GUESS CallerId resolves a contact name, a bare number, a genuinely withheld number, and "I am not allowed to look" - and keeps the last two apart. "I cannot see who is calling" and "the caller is unknown" are different claims, and collapsing them tells Kevin his caller withheld a number when the app was simply never permitted to check. Same shape as rendering a refused calendar permission as an empty day, which is settled decision 20. The announcement also stops offering what it cannot do: with no answer permission the prompt explicitly forbids offering to answer or decline. A BLOCKER FOUND BY TRACING, NOT BY TESTING isInCall was set true on RINGING, and LiveSessionController refuses to open a turn while isInCall - so the exact moment Kevin wants to say "answer it" was the moment the app showed "ON A CALL" and stopped listening. Voice answering was impossible before this and nothing would have reported that. Split into isRinging and isInCall: the proactive gate treats both as silence, the voice path deliberately does not. THE HONESTY PROBLEM acceptRingingCall() returns void. It reports nothing about whether the call was answered, so returning "probably fine" would push a lie one layer up into what the assistant says. CallActions instead WATCHES the phone's call state and reports what it observed: answering means RINGING became OFFHOOK. endCall does return a boolean and it is used, plus the same state check, because a true return is not the same as the ringing having stopped. That matters most for the case Android will not do at all: self-managed calls - WhatsApp, Signal, Teams - are silently ignored for a non-dialer app, with no error. The state check is what turns that silence into "that did not work, and here is why" instead of a confident false claim. Emergency calls cannot be ended either. Both named in the tool descriptions rather than discovered. Nine tests on the two describe() functions, which are the sentences that actually reach his ears. 1803 total, green. APK assembles, manifest merges. OWED on the phone: everything. Whether the number arrives, whether PhoneLookup matches his contacts, whether answering by voice beats the dialer UI to it, and whether the wake word can even be heard over a ringing phone - that last one is not addressed here and may well be the next problem. Also fixes a race introduced with the capture refactor: releasing cancelled the read loop without joining it, so the record was freed while a read was still in flight. Vosk's SpeechService joined its thread and did not have this bug. Now stop, then join (bounded 1s), then release - stop first is what makes the join fast.
